implementation_notes: std::sync::mpsc is the standard library's multi-producer, single-consumer FIFO queue: Sender is Clone but Receiver is not, so 'each value reaches one consumer' is enforced by ownership instead of convention. sync_channel(bound) is the bounded queue - send blocks at capacity and a bound of 0 is a rendezvous hand-off - and send/recv return Result, so a hung-up peer is a value rather than a panic. Tokio's mpsc is the async counterpart; durability still requires a broker client.
pitfalls: Receiver is neither Clone nor Sync: competing consumers must share it behind a Mutex (which serializes them), so real fan-out needs crossbeam-channel or one channel per worker.
recv() blocks; calling it inside an async task parks a runtime worker thread - use tokio::sync::mpsc there.
Sending after the receiver is dropped returns Err(SendError); unwrapping it away silently loses the message.

variants.name: tokio::sync::mpsc async channel
variants.implementation_notes: tokio::sync::mpsc is the async channel for request/reply inside a runtime: a bounded send awaits until capacity frees instead of blocking a thread, and the receiver keeps the single-consumer guarantee while Sender clones give fan-in. The docs are explicit that the bounded variant is the one that applies backpressure, and that the channel is runtime-agnostic and cooperates with the scheduler; prefer it in async services and keep the stdlib channel for pure thread code.
pitfalls: UnboundedSender never applies backpressure - the docs say so explicitly - so it converts overload into memory growth.
Dropping the Receiver drains and drops buffered messages; a clean shutdown closes the sender side, drains, then drops.
blocking_send/blocking_recv from inside the runtime is a runtime hazard rather than a compile error.
